jacamar.etymology: F. jacamar, Braz. jacamarica; cf. Sp. jacamar.

jacinth.etymology: F. jacinthe, L. hyacinthus. See Hyacinth.

jackal.etymology: Pers. shaghal: cf. OF. jackal, F. chacal; cf. Skr. ç\'f0gala.

jackanapes.etymology: For Jack o' (= of) apes; prop., a man who exhibits apes.

jacket.etymology: F. jaquette, dim. of jaque. See 3d Jack, n.

jacobean.etymology: From L. Jacobus James. See 2d Jack.

jacobite.etymology: L. Jacobus James: cf. F. Jacobite. See 2d Jack.

jactation.etymology: L. jactatio, fr. jactare: af. F. jactation. See Jactancy.

jactitation.etymology: L. jactitare to utter in public, from jactare. See Jactancy.

jade.etymology: F., fr. Sp. jade, fr. piedra de ijada stone of the side, fr. ijada flank, side, pain in the side, the stone being so named because it was supposed to cure this pain. Sp. ijada is derived fr. L. ilia flanks. Cf. Iliac.

jag.etymology: Prob. of Celtic origin; cf. W. gag aperture, cleft, chink; akin to Ir. & Gael. gag.

jail.etymology: OE. jaile, gail, gayhol, OF. gaole, gaiole, jaiole, F. geôle, LL. gabiola, dim. of gabia cage, for L. cavea cavity, cage. See Cage.

jailer.etymology: OE. jailer, gailer, OF. geolier, F. geôlier. See Jail.

jain.etymology: Skr. Jaina, fr. Jina, a proper name, fr. jina victorious.

jakes.etymology: Prob. fr. F. Jacques, the proper name. See 2d Jack.

jam.etymology: Per. or Hind. jamah garment, robe.

jamb.etymology: Prov. E. jaumb, jaum, F. jambe a leg, jambe de force a principal rafter. See Gambol.

jangle.etymology: OE. janglen to quarrel, OF. jangler to rail, quarrel; of Dutch or German origin; cf. D. jangelen, janken, to whimper, chide, brawl, quarrel.

january.etymology: L. Januarius, fr. Janus an old Latin deity, the god of the sun and the year, to whom the month of January was sacred; cf. janua a door, Skr. ya to go.

jape.etymology: Prob. from the same source as gab,influenced by F. japper to yelp. See Gab to deceive.

jargon.etymology: F. jargon, OF. also gargon, perh. akin to E. garrulous, or gargle.

jasmine.etymology: F. jasmin, Sp. jazmin, Ar. yasmin, Pers. yasmin; cf. It. gesmino, gelsomino. Cf. Jessamine.

jasper.etymology: OE. jaspre, jaspe, OF. jaspre, jaspe, F. jaspe, L. iaspis, Gr. yashp, yashf, Ar.yashb, yasb, yasf, Heb. yashpheh. Cf. Diaper.

jaundice.etymology: OE. jaunis, F. jaunisse, fr. jaune yellow, orig. jalne, fr. L. galbinus yellowish, fr. galbus yellow.

jaunt.etymology: Cf. Scot. jaunder to ramble, jaunt to taunt, jeer, dial. Sw. ganta to play the buffoon, romp, jest; perh. akin to E. jump. Cf. Jaunce.

jaunty.etymology: Formerly spelt janty, fr. F. gentil. See Gentle, and cf. Genty.

javelin.etymology: F. javeline; akin to Sp. jabalina, It. giavelina, and F. javelot, OF. gavlot. Cf. Gavelock.

jaw.etymology: A modification of chaw, formed under the influence of F. joue the cheek. See Chaw, Chew.

jay.etymology: F. geai, OF. gai, jaj, perh. fr. OHG. gahi. Cf. Gay.

jealous.etymology: OE. jalous, gelus, OF. jalous, F. jaloux, LL. zelosus zealous, fr. zelus emulation, zeal, jealousy, Gr. Zeal, and cf. Zealous.

jealousy.etymology: F. jalousie. See Jealous, and cf. Jalousie.

jean.etymology: Prob. named from Genoa. See Jane.

jehovah.etymology: Heb. usually yêhovah (with the vowel points of âdonai Lord), sometimes (to avoid repetition) yêhovih (with the vowel points of êlohim God); but only the four Heb, consonants yhvh are conceded to be certainly known.

jejune.etymology: L. jejunus fasting, hungry, dry, barren, scanty; of unknown origin.

jejunum.etymology: NL., fr. L. jejunus empty, dry.

jelly.etymology: Formerly gelly, gely, F. gelée jelly, frost, fr. geler to freeze. L. gelare; akin to gelu frost. See Gelid.

jennet.etymology: F. genet, Sp. jinete, orig., a mounted soldier, Ar. zenata a tribe of Barbary celebrated for its cavalry.

jenny.etymology: A corruption of gin an engine; influenced by Jenny, the proper name. See Gin an engine, and cf. Ginny-carriage.

jeopardy.etymology: OE. jupartie, juperti, jeuparti, OF. jeu parti an even game, a game in which the chances are even; OF. jeu, ju, F. jeu (L. jocus jest) + F. partier to divide, L. partire to divide. See Joke, and Part.

jeremiad.etymology: From Jeremiah, the prophet: cf. F. jérémiade.

jerk.etymology: Corrupted from Peruv. charqui dried beef.

jerkin.etymology: Dim. of D. jurk a frock.

jersey.etymology: From Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands.

jest.etymology: OE. jeste, geste, deed, action, story, tale, OF. geste, LL. gesta, orig., exploits, neut. pl. from L. gestus, p. p. of gerere to bear, carry, accomplish, perform; perh. orig., to make to come, bring, and perh. akin to E. come. Cf. Gest a deed, Register, n.

jesuit.etymology: F. Jésuite, Sp. Jesuita: cf. It. Gesuita.

jesus.etymology: L. Jesus, Gr. Yésh; Yah Jehovah + h to help.

jet.etymology: OF. jet, jayet, F. jaïet, jais, L. gagates, fr. Gr. [written also jeat, jayet.

jetsam.etymology: F. jeter to throw: cf. OF. getaison a throwing. Cf. Flotsam, Jettison.

jetty.etymology: F.jetée a pier, a jetty, a causeway. See Jet a shooting forth, and cf. Jutty.

jew.etymology: OF. Juis, pl., F. Juif, L. Judaeus, Gr. Y Judah, son of Jacob. Cf. Judaic.

jewel.etymology: OE. juel, jowel, OF. jouel, juel, joiel, F. joyau, dim. of OF. joie joy, jewel, F. joie joy. See Joy.

jewry.etymology: OE. Jewerie, OF. Juierie, F. Juiverie.

jezebel.etymology: From Jezebel, Heb. Izebel, the wife of Ahab king of Israel.

jib.etymology: Named from its shifting from side to side. See Jib, v. i.., Jibe.

jibe.etymology: Cf. Dan. gibbe, D. gijpen, v. i., and dial. Sw. gippa to jerk. Cf. Jib, n. & v. i.

jig.etymology: OF. gigue a stringed instrument, a kind of dance, F. gigue dance, tune, gig; of German origin; cf. MHG. gige fiddle, G. geige. Cf. Gig a fiddle, Gig a whirligig.

jilt.etymology: Contr. fr. Scot. jillet a giddy girl, a jill-flirt, dim. of jill a jill.

jingle.etymology: OE. gingelen, ginglen; prob. akin to E. chink; cf. also E. jangle.

jingo.etymology: Said to be a corruption of St. Gingoulph.

jinrikisha.etymology: Jap. jin man + riki power + sha carriage.

job.etymology: Prov. E. job, gob, n., a small piece of wood, v., to stab, strike; cf. E. gob, gobbet; perh. influenced by E. chop to cut off, to mince. See Gob.

jockey.etymology: Dim. of Jack, Scot. Jock; orig., a boy who rides horses. See 2d Jack.

jocose.etymology: L jocosus, fr. jocus joke. See Joke.

jocular.etymology: L. jocularis, fr. joculus, dim. of jocus joke. See Joke.

jocund.etymology: L. jocundus, jucundus, orig., helpful, fr. juvare to help. See Aid.

jocundity.etymology: L. jocunditas jucunditas. See Jocund, and cf. Jucundity.

jog.etymology: OE. joggen; cf. W. gogi to shake, and also E. shog, shock, v.

join.etymology: OE. joinen, joignen, F. joindre, fr. L. jungere to yoke, bind together, join; akin to jugum yoke. See Yoke, and cf. Conjugal, Junction, Junta.

joint.etymology: F. joint, fr. joindre, p. p. joint. See Join.

jointure.etymology: F. jointure a joint, orig., a joining, L. junctura, fr. jungere to join. See Join, and cf. Juncture.

joist.etymology: OE. giste, OF. giste, F. gîte, fr. gesir to lie, F. gésir. See Gist.

joke.etymology: L. jocus. Cf Jeopardy, Jocular, Juggler.

jollification.etymology: Jolly + L. -ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

jollity.etymology: From Jolly: cf. OF. jolieté, joliveté.

jolly.etymology: OF. joli, jolif, joyful, merry, F. joli pretty; of Scand. origin, akin to E. yule; cf. Icel. j yule, Christmass feast. See Yule.

jolt.etymology: Prob. fr. jole, joll, jowl, and orig. meaning, to knock on the head. See Jowl.

jonquil.etymology: F. jonquille, fr. L. juncus a rush, because it has rushlike leaves.

jordan.etymology: Prob. fr. the river Jordan, and shortened fr. Jordan bottle a bottle of water from the Jordan, brought back by pilgrims.

jorum.etymology: Perh. corrupted fr. jorden an earthen pot.

joss.etymology: Chinese, corrupt. fr. Pg. deos God, L. deus.

jostle.etymology: A dim. of joust, just, v. See Joust, and cf. Justle.

jot.etymology: L. iota, Gr. i. Heb. y), the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet. Cf. Iota.

joule.etymology: From the distinguished English physicist, James P. Joule.

journal.etymology: F., fr. L. diurnalis diurnal, fr. diurnus belonging to the day, fr. dies day. See Diurnal.

journey.etymology: OE. jornee, journee, prop., a day's journey, OF. jornée, jurnée, a day, a day's work of journey, F. journée, fr. OF. jorn, jurn, jor a day, F. jour, fr. L. diurnus. See Journal.

joust.etymology: OE. justen, jousten, OF. jouster, jouster, joster, F. jouter, fr. L. juxta near to, nigh, from the root of jungere to join. See Join, and cf. Jostle.

jove.etymology: L. Jupiter, gen. Jovis, OL. Jovis, nom. & gen. for Djovis; akin to E. Tuesday. See Tuesday, and cf. Jupiter.

jovial.etymology: F., fr. L. Jovialis pertaining to Jove. The planet Jupiter was thought to make those born under it joyful or jovial. See Jove.

jowl.etymology: For older chole, chaul, AS. ceaft jaw. Cf. Chaps.

joy.etymology: OE. joye, OF. joye, joie, goie, F. joie, L. gaudia, pl. of gaudium joy, fr. gaudere to rejoice, to be glad; cf. Gr. Gaud, Jewel.

joyous.etymology: OE. joyous, joious, joios, F. joyeux.See Joy.

jubilant.etymology: L. jubilans, -antis, p. pr. of jubilare to shout for joy: cf. F. jubila. See Jubilate.

jubilate.etymology: L., imperat. of jubilare to shout for joy.

jubilee.etymology: F. jubilé, L. jubilaeus, Gr. y the blast of a trumpet, also the grand sabbatical year, which was announced by sound of trumpet.

judaic.etymology: L. Judaïcus, fr. Judaea, the country Judea: cf. F. Judaïque. See Jew.

judaical.etymology: L. Judaïcus, fr. Judaea, the country Judea: cf. F. Judaïque. See Jew.

judge.etymology: OE. juge, OF. & F. juge, fr. OF. jugier, F. juger, to judge. See Judge, v. i.

judgment.etymology: OE. jugement, F. jugement, LL. judicamentum, fr. L. judicare. See Judge, v. i.

judicable.etymology: L. judicabilis. See Judge, v. i.

judicial.etymology: L. judicialis, fr. judicium judgment, fr. judex judge: cf. OF. judicial. See Judge.

judiciary.etymology: L. judiciarius, fr. judicium judgment: cf. F. judiciare. See Judicial.

judicious.etymology: F. judicieux, fr. L. judicium judgment. See Judicial.

jug.etymology: Prob. fr. Jug, a corruption of, or nickname for, Joanna; cf. 2d Jack, and Jill. See Johannes.

juggernaut.etymology: Skr. jagannatha lord of the world.

juggle.etymology: OE. juglen; cf. OF. jogler, jugler, F. jongler. See Juggler.

juggler.etymology: OE. jogelour, juglur, OF. jogleor, jugleor, jongleor, F. jongleur, fr. L. joculator a jester, joker, fr. joculus a little jest or joke, dim. of jocus jest, joke. See Joke, and cf. Jongleur, Joculator.

jugular.etymology: L. jugulum the collar bone, which joins together the shoulders and the breast, the throat, akin to jungere to yoke, to join: cf. F. jugulaire. See Join.

juice.etymology: OE. juse, F.jus broth, gravy, juice, L. jus; akin to Skr. y.

jujube.etymology: F., fr. L. zizyphum, Gr. zizf, zizaf, zayzaf.

julep.etymology: F., fr. Sp. julepe, fr. Ar. & Per. julab, jullab, fr. Per. gulab rose water and julep; gul rose + ab water.

julian.etymology: L. Julianus, fr. Julius. Cf. July, Gillian.

july.etymology: L.Julius; -- named from Caius Julius Cæsar, who was born in this month: cf. F. Juillet.

jumble.etymology: Prob. fr. jump, i. e., to make to jump, or shake.

jument.etymology: L. jumentum a beast of burden: cf. F. jument a mare, OF., a beast of burden.

jump.etymology: Cf. F. jupe a long petticoat, a skirt. Cf. Juppon.

junction.etymology: L. junctio, fr. jungere, junctum, to join: cf. F. jonction. See Join.

juncture.etymology: L.junctura, fr. jungere to join. See Jointure.

june.etymology: L. Junius: cf. F. Juin. So called either from Junius, the name of a Roman gens, or from Juno, the goddess.

jungle.etymology: Hind. jangal desert, forest, jungle; Skr. ja desert.

junior.etymology: L. contr. fr. juvenior, compar. of juvenis young. See Juvenile.

juniper.etymology: L. juniperus, prop., youth-producing, and so called from its evergreen appearance, from the roots of E. juvenile, and parent. Cf. Gin the liquor.

junk.etymology: Pg. junco junk, rush, L. juncus a bulrush, of which ropes were made in early ages. Cf. Junket.

junket.etymology: Formerly also juncate, fr. It. giuncata cream cheese, made in a wicker or rush basket, fr. L. juncus a rush. See 2d Junk, and cf. Juncate.

junta.etymology: Sp., fr. L. junctus joined, p. p. of jungere to join. See Join, and cf. Junto.

jupiter.etymology: L., fr. Jovis pater. See Jove.

juridic.etymology: L. juridicus relating to the administration of justice; jus, juris, right, law + dicare to pronounce: cf. F. juridique. See Just, a., and Diction.

juridical.etymology: L. juridicus relating to the administration of justice; jus, juris, right, law + dicare to pronounce: cf. F. juridique. See Just, a., and Diction.

jurisdiction.etymology: L. jurisdictio; jus, juris, right, law + dictio a saying, speaking: cf. OF. jurisdiction, F. juridiction. See Just, a., and Diction.

jurisprudence.etymology: L. jurisprudentia; jus, juris, right, law + prudentia a foreseeing, knowledge of a matter, prudence: cf. F. jurisprudence. See Just, a., and Prudence.

jurist.etymology: F. juriste, LL. jurista, fr. L. jus, juris, right, law. See Just, a.

juror.etymology: F. jureur one who takes oath, L. jurator a swearer, fr. jurare, jurari, to swear. See Jury, n.

just.etymology: F. juste, L. justus, fr. jus right, law, justice; orig., that which is fitting; akin to Skr. yu to join. Cf. Injury, Judge, Jury, Giusto.

justice.etymology: F., fr. L. justitia, fr. justus just. See Just, a.

justiciary.etymology: Cf. LL. justitiarius, F. justicier. See Justice.

justification.etymology: L. justificatio: cf. F. justification. See Justify.

justify.etymology: F. justifier, L. justificare; justus just + - ficare (in comp.) to make. See Just, a., and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

jute.etymology: Hind. j, Skr. j matted hair; cf. ja matted hair, fibrous roots.

juvenal.etymology: L. juvenalis youthful, juvenile, fr. juvenis young.

juvenile.etymology: L. juvenilis, from juvenis young; akin to E. young: cf. F. juvénile, juvénil. See Young.

juxtaposition.etymology: L. juxta near + positio position: cf. F. juxtaposition. See Just, v. i., and Position.
